vignette:
# Chinedu's Assault and Its Aftermath

Chinedu Okafor was twenty-two when three men cornered him outside a bar in downtown Baltimore on a Friday night in March. He had gone out with colleagues from the urban planning firm where he had been working for eight months—his first real job after graduating from Howard University with high hopes of redesigning neglected neighborhoods. The bar was near the Inner Harbor, a place his coworkers frequented. He remembered the evening as a series of frozen images: the smell of spilled beer and whiskey, thick and sweet; the sudden shift in the bar's energy when a group of men at the next table began arguing; the moment he decided to leave early because the noise made him uneasy; the alley behind the building where he had stepped to call an Uber.

What happened next existed in his mind as three distinct photographs. The first: a face very close to his, twisted with rage, alcohol on the man's breath. The second: his own body hitting the brick wall, the impact traveling through his spine. The third: his hands up, useless, unable to stop anything. He had been hit repeatedly, his wallet taken, his ribs bruised. The police arrived within minutes of a passerby's call, but by then the men had scattered. The officers took his statement in a flat, procedural manner. One detective suggested he should not have been alone in that alley at that hour. Another implied the assault might have been gang-related, though Chinedu had no gang affiliation. The case remained open but inactive. No arrests were made.

In the weeks after, Chinedu's world contracted. The startle responses began almost immediately—a car horn would send his heart racing; the sound of raised voices on the street outside his apartment made him flinch as though the blow was coming again. He could not trust that he was safe even in his own home. When his mother called from Lagos and assured him he was far from danger now, he heard her words but could not believe them. The alcohol smell became a physical trigger; he could smell it on strangers' breath in the Metro, on the clothes of people passing him on the sidewalk, and each time it transported him back to that face, that rage.

By late spring, Chinedu had begun avoiding situations where conflict might emerge. At work, when his supervisor questioned his designs for a community revitalization project, Chinedu's instinct was to withdraw rather than defend his ideas. He found himself unable to push back, to assert himself, to occupy space. He came to believe that he could not handle even the smallest disagreement—that any confrontation would unravel him completely. He started taking longer routes to avoid the bar district entirely, which meant adding twenty minutes to his commute. He stopped attending team lunches.

The rumination consumed him. He replayed his own choices obsessively: Why had he gone to that bar? Why had he stepped outside alone? Why had he not fought back harder? He had come to believe that he had done something fundamentally wrong, that his own failure of judgment had caused this. To escape the spiral of self-blame, he began gambling online—betting on football matches, playing poker sites late into the night. The distraction worked briefly, the rush of potential winnings pulling him away from the memory, but it cost him money he did not have. He had already lost nearly three thousand dollars by July.

The memory itself was fragmented and overwhelming. When it returned—which it did several times a day—he could see the three moments clearly, each one vivid and separate, but he could not string them into a coherent narrative. When his therapist at the university counseling center asked him to describe what happened, the words simply would not come. He knew what had occurred, but the gap between knowing and telling felt unbridgeable. The emotion that flooded him on recall was so intense that he had to stop, to leave the session, to sit in his car for an hour before he could drive home.

By September, six months after the assault, Chinedu had withdrawn from two major projects at work and was on the verge of being placed on a performance improvement plan. His supervisor had noticed his absence from meetings and his reluctance to present ideas. His colleagues had stopped inviting him to social events. He had not been on a date since the assault. He felt utterly helpless—certain that bad things would happen to him and equally certain that nothing he did could stop them.

It was his mother's voice on a video call that finally pushed him to seek help. She said he sounded like someone who was drowning, and she was right. Chinedu called a trauma-informed therapist and made his first appointment. What he wanted most was to feel safe again, to trust his own judgment, to walk through the world without flinching. What he feared most was that he never would.
